58-002.r: Botulism (food poisoning) → toxin of Clostridium botulinum bacteria growing in improperly canned or preserved food; can also enter through wounds.

58-003.r: Botulism → food-borne intoxication: Clostridium botulinum toxin attacks nerves → breathing difficulty, muscle paralysis, death; bacteria thrive in low-oxygen home-canned food.
58-003.t: Intoxication (toxin already in food), not infection.

58-004.r: Splenic fever = anthrax, a bacterial infection that enlarges the spleen; affects livestock and can pass to humans.

58-005.r: Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) vaccine → toxoid vaccine; it cut cases by more than 90% between 1980 and 2000.

58-006.r: DPT (triple antigen) → diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough) and tetanus, all bacterial; not used for polio.

58-011.r: Haemophilus influenzae (a bacterium) causes meningitis in young children and pneumonia – book gives two answers, (a) and (d); flu itself is caused by influenza viruses.

58-012.r: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (Streptococcus pneumoniae) → at least 80% effective against pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis; reduce antibiotic-resistant disease (1, 2 true); 'no side effects' is false.

58-013.r: Tuberculosis → bacterial (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), generally affects lungs; measles, rabies, polio are viral.

58-014.r: Rifampicin treats both tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) and leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae, in multidrug therapy); the book prints P-amino salicylic acid, a TB-only drug.
58-014.c: Rifampicin, option (d), is the standard drug for both TB and leprosy (part of leprosy multidrug therapy); PAS is a TB drug, not used for leprosy.

58-015.r: WHO: tuberculosis kills the most people (outside the COVID-19 period) – 1.25 million deaths in 2023, including 3.23 lakh in India.

58-017.r: Wrong pair: tuberculosis – genetic disease (TB is bacterial, Mycobacterium tuberculosis). Correct: rheumatoid arthritis – autoimmune; scabies – mite; schizophrenia – mental.

58-020.r: Mantoux (book: Montoux) tuberculin skin test → detects tuberculosis; tuberculin is injected into the skin of the lower arm.

58-021.r: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin) vaccine → prevents tuberculosis; given just after birth.

58-022.r: BCG vaccine (against T.B.) should be given just after birth; it can be given up to 12 months of age, but works less if late.

58-024.r: Correct pair: malaria – chloroquine. Wrong: scurvy is vitamin C lack (thiamine is vitamin B); BCG → TB; ATS (tetanus antitoxin) → tetanus.

58-025.r: Tetanus = 'lockjaw': Clostridium tetani toxin from a wound tightens neck and jaw muscles, making it hard to open the mouth or swallow.

58-026.r: Plague → bacterium Yersinia pestis, spread among rodents and to humans by fleas, not mosquitoes; yellow fever, malaria, dengue are mosquito-borne.

58-027.r: By air → T.B.; by water → cholera; by contact → syphilis; by wound → tetanus.

58-028.r: Tuberculosis : lungs :: typhoid : intestines (especially the small intestine).

58-029.r: Plague → flea bites; filaria → mosquitoes; beri-beri → vitamin B deficiency; typhoid → affects the intestines.

58-030.r: Tooth decay (dental caries) → bacteria acting on carbohydrate food particles; needs tooth surface, bacteria, fermentable carbohydrates (e.g. sucrose) and time.

58-032.r: Shallow handpump water → cholera, typhoid, jaundice (microbes); fluorosis comes from excess fluoride, not microbes.

58-033.r: Cholera → waterborne diarrhoeal illness caused by Vibrio cholerae, from contaminated water or food.

58-034.r: Typhoid and cholera → waterborne diseases; prevented by proper treatment of drinking water; about 4 million die yearly from water-related diseases.

58-035.r: Leprosy (Hansen's disease) → long-term infection by bacteria Mycobacterium leprae or Mycobacterium lepromatosis.

58-036.r: Typhoid → Salmonella typhi bacteria; jaundice, influenza and mumps are viral (per book).

58-037.r: Term 'antibiotic' coined by Selman Waksman in 1942; he also discovered streptomycin.

58-038.r: Antibiotics among options: chloramphenicol and sulphaguanidine (a sulphonamide) → 'more than one' (e).

58-039.r: Antibiotics among options: penicillin and sulphadiazine (a sulphonamide) → 'more than one' (e).

58-041.r: Penicillin → discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928: the mould Penicillium notatum inhibited bacterial growth.

58-042.r: Broad-spectrum antibiotic → chloramphenicol (chloronitromycin): acts on both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.

58-043.r: Sulfa drugs (from sulfanilamide) → synthetic antibacterials for bacterial infections, largely replaced by antibiotics; e.g. sulfadiazine, sulfacetamide.

58-045.r: Cibazole → short-acting sulpha drug, effective on Gram-positive and Gram-negative microbes; no longer used in humans but used in cattle.

58-046.r: Multi-drug resistance in India (DBT report, November 2017): incorrect antibiotic doses and antibiotics in livestock farming (2, 3); not genetics or chronic diseases.

59-001.r: Mucormycosis (zygomycosis) → rare fungal infection, not zoonotic; rabies, plague and SARS are zoonotic (pathogen jumps from animal to human).

59-002.r: Ergotism → eating grains (rye, other cereals) contaminated by alkaloids of the fungus Claviceps purpurea.

59-003.r: Athlete's foot (Tinea pedis) → fungal infection between the toes (Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum).

59-004.r: True: femur is the longest bone; cholera is bacterial (Vibrio cholerae). False: athlete's foot is fungal, not viral.

59-005.r: Seborrheic dermatitis → fungal inflammatory skin disorder of scalp, face, torso; polio is viral, cholera bacterial.

59-006.r: Among options, baldness → fungal disease (book); AIDS → HIV virus; colour blindness → genetic disorder.
59-006.c: Common baldness is mainly hereditary or hormonal; only patchy hair loss from fungal scalp infection (ringworm) is fungal, which is what the answer intends.

59-007.r: Aflatoxins (from fungi Aspergillus and Penicillium) make food toxic and mainly damage the liver.

60-001.r: Malaria → Plasmodium parasite carried by female Anopheles mosquito; most affected organ is the spleen (enlarges); quinine is the traditional drug.

60-004.r: Anopheles mosquitoes, besides malaria, carry encephalitis (JEV, e.g. Anopheles subpictus; Culex is the main vector) and filariasis.

60-005.r: Malignant (most severe) malaria → Plasmodium falciparum; higher risk of death.

60-007.r: Malaria and dengue differ in mosquito species: malaria → female Anopheles; dengue → female Aedes aegypti.

60-008.r: Malaria → caused by the protozoan Plasmodium; female Anopheles mosquito is its carrier (secondary host).

60-010.r: Not true: 'malaria is caused by an insect parasite' – Plasmodium is a protozoan. True: spread by mosquitoes, common in swampy areas, treated with chloroquine.

60-011.r: P. vivax → about 65% of malaria cases in India (also Asia, South America); most widespread cause of recurring malaria; one of five malaria parasites.

60-012.r: Sir Ronald Ross (British Indian Army doctor) found Plasmodium oocysts in the female Anopheles mosquito; Nobel prize 1902.

60-013.r: R21/Matrix-M → malaria vaccine by Oxford's Jenner Institute and Serum Institute of India; second malaria vaccine for children; WHO-recommended October 2023.

60-014.r: Filaria (filariasis) → thread-like nematodes (roundworms, Filarioidea) spread by female Culex mosquito; edema is a common symptom.

60-015.r: Wrong set: Aedes – chikungunya – bacteria; chikungunya is viral (CHIKV, RNA alphavirus). Correct: Culex – filariasis – parasite; Anopheles – malaria; Aedes – dengue – virus.

60-016.r: Malaria → protozoan; poliomyelitis → virus; tuberculosis → bacteria; ringworm → fungi.

60-017.r: Plague → bacteria; AIDS → virus; baldness → fungus; malaria → protozoa.

60-018.r: Peptic ulcers → bacteria; dengue → virus; elephant foot (filaria) → worm; malaria → protozoa.
